bib.title: Chapter 5. Vector Databases with FAISS and Pinecone (from Prompt Engineering for Generative AI)

question: How can embeddings and vector databases (FAISS locally, Pinecone hosted) supply relevant context to a prompt at runtime, and what choices (embedding model, chunking, metadata, retriever type) shape the result?
contributions: Introduces embeddings, vector search and the RAG pattern (chunk, index, search, insert into prompt).
Worked code for embeddings (OpenAI, Sentence Transformers, word2vec, TF-IDF), chunking, FAISS, LangChain LCEL RAG, Pinecone, and self-querying retrieval.
Compares hosted and open source vector stores and lists alternative LangChain retrievers with their trade-offs.

results.claim: A very large chunk's embedding regresses toward the mean and carries little semantic information, while very small chunks lose meaning when cut mid-sentence; chunking is described as much of the art of working with vector databases.

For heavy workloads the up-front cost of fine-tuning a custom model may beat the ongoing cost of prompts plus embeddings plus vector storage, and vector search adds cost and latency that should be tested.

limits: No experiment compares chunk sizes, overlaps, embedding models or vector stores; every result is a toy example (an invented employee handbook, four or nine toy sentences).
Prices, the choice of ada-002 as 'the standard model', Pinecone as 'the current leader' and gpt-4-1106-preview are dated and tied to the time of writing.
The word2vec example is conceded to be cherry-picked via the seed ('If you remove that seed, you'll find it rarely discovers the association').
FAISS index merging via reconstruct_n works for flat indexes only and does not carry IDs; the chapter says it may not work for IndexIVFFlat or indexes with different configurations.
Only IndexFlatL2 (brute force) is shown; no approximate indexes (IVF, HNSW), recall or latency numbers.
The chapter says a vector search is 'not necessary' in many cases; retrieval may use traditional database search or web browsing.
practices: Use RAG: chunk documents, index chunks in a vector database, search by vector, insert records into the prompt as context (RAG section).
Embed smaller chunks when close similarity matters, but not so small that meaning is cut mid-sentence; chunking is much of the art (end of Introducing Embeddings).
Use a recursive character text splitter with token-based sizing and overlap (example chunk_size=100, chunk_overlap=20) to keep paragraphs, then sentences, together (Document Loading).
Budget the context window: reserve tokens for template and completion, then fill the rest with the top-k chunks (Document Loading, gpt-4-0613 example).
Store vectors rather than recomputing them; save and reload FAISS indexes with write_index and read_index (Memory Retrieval with FAISS).
Set a system message that tells the model to answer only from the supplied context and to say 'I don't know' otherwise (Memory Retrieval with FAISS, search_and_chat).
Use the same embedding model for documents and queries; vectors are not comparable across models or model versions (Introducing Embeddings).
Use TF-IDF for small document sets instead of training word2vec, which needs tens of millions of words (Introducing Embeddings).
Consider training a custom embedding model when the domain vocabulary differs from general usage (Introducing Embeddings).
Upsert in batches with retry on rate-limit errors (batch_size 10 in the example, 100 for real workloads) (Hosted Vector Databases with Pinecone).
Design a metadata strategy as carefully as a chunking strategy, and use metadata filters to scope similarity search (Hosted Vector Databases with Pinecone).
Weigh hosted databases (maintenance, scalability, reliability, support, security) against cost overspend, vendor lock-in and privacy (Hosted Vector Databases with Pinecone).
Use a self-querying retriever with temperature 0 so the metadata filter generation is consistent (Self-Querying).
Test whether the additional context from vector search is worth its cost and latency (Alternative Retrieval Mechanisms).

terms.definition: A tool most commonly used for storing text data in a way that enables querying based on similarity or semantic meaning.
the abstract multidimensional space formed by the model's parameters
Typically involves searching by similarity to the query, retrieving the most relevant documents, and inserting them into the prompt as context.
The vector representation of the text returned from a pretrained AI model.
The process of retrieving or generating embeddings; computing or retrieving the numerical (vector) representations of text from a model and storing them in a variable for later use.
Breaking down a text into smaller, manageable pieces or chunks to facilitate processing.
Vectors where each number in the array is almost always nonzero (i.e., they contain semantic information).
Vectors with a large number of dimensions (e.g., 100,000+) with many of the dimensions having a value of zero.
Search using both dense and sparse vectors.
A statistical measure used to evaluate the importance of a word in a document relative to a collection of documents.
A combination of update and insert: it either updates an existing record or inserts a new record if the record does not already exist.
A retriever that extracts metadata filters from the user's query and generates a new query to execute against the vector database, combining semantic similarity with metadata filtering.
